sections.overview: The Madagascar flying fox is the largest bat of Madagascar and is found nowhere else. It is a fruit bat that roosts in groups in trees and is listed as Vulnerable, mainly because of hunting and the loss of its forest.
sections.identification: A large bat with a body about 24–25 cm long, a wingspan of roughly 1.2 m and a mass of 500–750 g, males being heavier than females. It has a long pointed muzzle, pointed ears, large eyes and no obvious tail. The upper body is yellowish brown, the underside dark brown, the face and throat seal-brown and the neck yellowish to reddish brown.
sections.habitat: It lives only in Madagascar. It is described as roosting mainly in humid coastal forest on sandy soil, from sea level to about 800 m. In the Mangoro valley, in the centre-east, roosts were in small, isolated fragments of degraded humid forest of 2.2–28.7 ha and in two Eucalyptus plantations, all outside protected areas.
sections.diet: It mostly chews fruit to drink the juice and spits out the dry pulp and seeds. It also eats pollen and leaves, and sometimes insects. In the Mangoro valley, droppings contained remains of native forest trees, cultivated fruits and Eucalyptus flowers, so it can feed in landscapes changed by people.
sections.behavior: It roosts in groups of hundreds to thousands, often at the same site all year, but is very sensitive to disturbance and may move away. Numbers at a roost vary a lot from month to month: in the Mangoro valley only two of six sites held bats at every visit. In the mating season, dominant males defend territories on the roost trees. It relies mainly on scent and sound rather than echolocation.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place in April–May, with males gripping the female’s scruff. Gestation is given as 100–150 days, and delayed implantation is possible. Usually a single pup is born, around October, and is nursed for four to five months. Both sexes mature at 1.5 to 2 years. Three Mangoro roosts were occupied only from September to March, possibly as nursery roosts.
sections.ecology: It is an important seed disperser for many plants of the coastal forests, and the only fruit-eater there able to carry seeds over long distances, which may help link forest fragments. Pollen found on its body suggests it also pollinates some plants. Young that fall from the roost are taken by the Madagascar harrier-hawk.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Hunting for bushmeat was found at three of the Mangoro roosts, and fire and forest clearance are widespread; the authors of that study noted that no conservation plan existed for the species. Hunting also targets roosts and feeding trees elsewhere, and only some roosts are formally protected.
